newsitem.title: USA: Toyota '97 U.S. market share gains to be modest.
newsitem.headline: Toyota '97 U.S. market share gains to be modest.

text.p: Toyota Motor Corp is looking for modest market share gains in the U.S. in 1997, the company's top U.S. official said Saturday, disputing claims the weak yen will allow Japanese automakers to grab huge new slices of the American market.

"People overstate the impact of the yen on our pricing," Yale Gieszl, executive vice president of Toyota Motor Sales U.S.A. Inc told reporters at a news briefing following a speech to the National Automobile Dealers Association's annual convention.

Gieszl said more than 60 percent of the products Toyota sells in the U.S. are built in this country. Of those that are exported from Japan, he said the high cost of energy and raw materials in Japan offset the gains Toyota gets from the exchange rate.
"It's not like it's a one on one relationship," he said.

Then yen has been trading at about 120 to the U.S. dollar. A weaker yen makes it cheaper for Japanese automakers to produce vehicles in Japan, compared to what it costs Detroit's Big Three to make vehicles in the U.S.

Last week, Ford Motor Co chief financial officer John Devine said he believes the Japanese automakers are using the weak yen to boost their market share. Devine said that should start to show up in the January sales figures.
But in Toyota's case, Gieszl said the company is severly constrained by its U.S. production capacity, which is running at full volume.
"If we hit our targets, I'm looking for a modest increase" in market share, he said. "It depends on the size of the market though, because our sales growth is going to be somewhat limited."

Gieszl said Toyota expects its calendar year 1997 U.S. sales to be about flat compared with 1,160,000 vehicles it sold in 1996. Toyota is limited in how much it can export popular vehicles such as the 4Runner and RAV4 sport/utilities from Japan because of demand for those products elswhere, he said.
